tagline: Working ferries link island towns through the sheltered Inside Passage.
intro: Alaska’s Marine Highway carries people, freight and vehicles aboard state ferries, reaching Southeast communities without road access. Its routes collectively form an All-American Road; Alaska’s transportation department highlights the Inside Passage’s fjords, islands and forests of hemlock and spruce. More than 1,500 islands shelter that passage from large Pacific surges. These are working transportation links: the Southeast network combines mainline voyages typically lasting more than a day with shorter routes whose boats return to their home ports the same day.

The network began with a much smaller connection: in 1948, Haines residents Steve Homer and Ray Gelotte founded Chilkoot Motorship Lines. Their converted landing craft ran weekly from Tee Harbor to Haines and Skagway, linking the territorial capital with the international road system. The territory bought the line in 1951; in 1959, voters approved an $18 million bond package for vessels and docks. The southern terminus moved from Seattle to Bellingham in 1989.

Follow the Inside Passage portion south from Skagway through Haines and Juneau, then Petersburg, Wrangell and Ketchikan toward Bellingham. Along this journey, Alaska’s byway account points to Skagway’s Klondike history, Petersburg’s fishing community and Wrangell’s concentration of petroglyphs. For the whole ferry byway, the Federal Highway Administration describes trips ranging from single-day excursions to several weeks.

moments.title: Skagway
moments.text: Skagway’s port stands at the beginning of a railway built during the Klondike gold rush. On July 29, 1897, the steamer Queen brought the first boatload of prospectors to Moore’s wharf. The White Pass and Yukon Route began laying narrow-gauge tracks in May 1898. By the time the railroad was completed in 1900, the rush was nearly over. The town occupies a narrow glaciated valley at the head of Taiya Inlet. Its historic district contains about 100 gold-rush-era buildings. The White Pass and Yukon Route now runs narrow-gauge passenger trains from the port during the summer months.

moments.title: Petersburg
moments.text: Icebergs from LeConte Glacier once supplied Petersburg’s fishing port with ice to cool its catch. In the nineteenth century, Norwegian immigrant Peter Buschmann built a cannery, sawmill and docks here; the settlement took his name. Scandinavian immigration gave the town its nickname, Little Norway. Petersburg celebrates Norwegian Constitution Day with Mayfest on the third weekend in May. Commercial fishing remains the main driver of the economy. The town sits at the north end of Mitkof Island, where Wrangell Narrows meets Frederick Sound. It is also the headquarters of the Petersburg Indian Association, a federally recognized tribe of Tlingit people.

moments.title: Petroglyph Beach, Wrangell
moments.text: Whales, salmon and faces appear in carvings on Wrangell’s shore. At Petroglyph Beach, barely a mile out of town, at least 40 petroglyphs have been found. They occupy boulders and bedrock outcrops just above and below mean high tide. The carvings are thought to have been made by members of the Tlingit tribe. The beach became a State Historic Park in 2000. Alaska’s transportation department identifies it as Southeast Alaska’s highest concentration of petroglyphs. The metamorphic rock tends to be dark gray and finely grained; Wikipedia suggests that its ease of fracture would have helped the carvers work it.
moments.notice: Look for carved figures on shore boulders and bedrock above and below mean high tide.
